utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I must start the day by raising a problem that my infallible assistant has noticed. We admitted yesterday as an exhibit P996, the statement of Witness Drewienkiewicz given in 2000. The version disclosed to us was redacted and from it the following paragraphs are missing: From 147 through 154. And the Defence team worked with that version. However, the version in e-court contains these paragraphs, and that's the version that has been admitted. I believe this is not appropriate. I don't know if the same version was given to the Trial Chamber as the one given to the Defence, but I believe the version admitted and the one uploaded into the e-court should be the one that we have, the version identical for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case manager, Ms. Pedersen, is telling me that we have disclosed the full version of this witness statement. We are checking our records for the exact date of that. The redacted version that my learned colleague is referring to is a version that was admitted in the Milutinovic trial. That version had initially been incorrectly uploaded in the e-court system that was corrected last week, and -- so we have the complete version of this witness statement in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In summary, the wrong version has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, the correct version was admitted and provided to the Defence. All I'm saying is that if my learned colleague's printed out the version that was in e-court somewhere before the beginning of last week, they would have had the wrong version because we corrected the e-court system -- the copy in e-court system just at the beginning of -- sometime last week. I don't remember exactly which day that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I don't think we need to spend more time on it now. You should have the version with all the paragraphs, not the redacted version. If you haven't, if you would consult with the court officer somewhere, you have a earlier redacted version and that could be overcome. The formal admitted document is not redacted, it has everything. If by tomorrow morning you haven't been able to find the correct one, raise it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm being told by Ms. Pedersen that the records shows that the full version was disclosed in December 2007. It's been available to the Defence since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What's available and what's admitted are two different things. We want to be sure the correct version is admitted and that the correct version is shown on e-court to Defence and anybody else who looks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was the case, Your Honour. That was the correct version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we leave it with you then, Mr. Djurdjic. Thank you. That's one problem. While the witness is being brought in, we cannot as Judges get today's transcript on our screen. We have yesterday's.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I already informed the technician. They are coming to fix it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made yesterday to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have back up on the screen Exhibit P1011 which was the last document we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn to tab 17 again of your binder. Yesterday when we with left off we were looking at this document, and I would ask you to turn to the last page, the almost-to-last paragraph of the document. I'm just going to check if the document is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have the last page of it displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you for a clarification of what is stated in the first sentence of this page where it says: "6 to 8 K enter FYROM yesterday reported to be up to 50 K waiting to cross in the immediate border area. This morning we have seen a further 7 K arrive by train." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to thousands of displaced persons. 6.000 to 8.000 entered FYROM yesterday. There were reported to be up to 50.000 waiting to cross an immediate border area. This morning we've seen a further 7.000 arrive by train. So that was just my shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what would have been the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers would have come through to me from my people on the ground because I had people at the border watching what was going on. I will be the first to admit that the exact numbers are subject to -- were the judgement of the people that were there, but they had spent quite a long time there by then, and they had got quite used to seeing several thousand. So I think they were very capable of knowing what 1.000 people looked like milling around in a muddy field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just for clarification, what does FYROM stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, the country to the south of Serbia and to the south of Kosovo and that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have up on the screen 02541.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is tab 18 of your binder. And I would ask that you turn to that. I see we have the document up on the screen. Sir, I would just ask if you could tell us what this document is, if you know, and I'm particularly interested in a bullet point that's dated 20 March, 2009 which starts with "Evacuation of OSCE KVM."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was another version of the previous serial. This was, I think, the first draft of it on the assumption that I would have to brief people who were utterly unaware of the situation and therefore I needed to have one page in which everything that had happened starting the previous October was set out. And so the aim, the buildup, the current situation, were really the three issues. And as you saw in the previous serial, the buildup part of that was -- was not used in the briefing that eventually took place. The 20th of March, which was the day we were ordered out, and as it says, "The start of unconstrained operations by MUP and VJ against civilians especially in the Podujevo area." Our authority for saying that or -- my authority for saying that was that as we were driving out, we were already seeing VJ and MUP forces leaving their areas in columns and headed out towards the areas where KLA were known to be. There was also a number of agencies, particularly UNHCR, that stayed an extra day after we stayed, and they didn't evacuate until the next day, the 21st. And when they came out, they reported to us that the moment we had left, in their words, all hell broke loose; and therefore, what we saw of people leaving their barrack areas was confirmed by the UNHCR in particular as they remained there throughout the next 24 hours. And the level of violence went up to such a degree that the UNHCR promptly left because they had -- they had felt that although we were ordered out that they had a duty to stay, despite our having left until the level of violence became so great that they too had to leave for their own safety. And that took just 24 hours before that decision was made by them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were -- received this reports that the level of violence had increased, what exactly were you told was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were told that the areas we were all familiar with were subject to attacks by the various Serb forces that had been leaving barracks as we were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It is 02541, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would now like to have P840 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, we're going to have a photograph displayed on the screen right before you. We are no longer going to be referring to the binder that you have there, so you can just close that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would just like to ask you if you recognise the locality that's shown in the photograph and if you can provide any comments as to what is seen there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could please zoom in for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the area immediately south of the border crossing from Kosovo into Macedonia at Brezda due south of Djeneral Jankovic. It's the view from the main road which runs along the bottom edge of this photo. I would say it's about the 2nd of April because it's not the moment that everybody arrived because you can see that there are some fires that have been lit for cooking, and there have been some temporary shelters put up by the people. And when we first saw this about 24 hours before, there were no fires, there were no shelters. It was just people stumbling around in that area. And the people there are Kosovar Albanians who have just arrived here by walking down the railway line which is at the top right-hand corner of this picture. I think the picture was probably taken by Richard Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you yourself travel to this area to see this field with refugees that we see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there the day before this. After I -- after I was in the Ministry of Defence in the UK, I was put on a plane to be taken straight back to Macedonia. And I think I landed soon after lunch the next day. And when I landed, the first thing that happened was I got a call on mobile phone from Richard Ciaglinski who said, Hey, you need to come and see this because it has got a lot worse since you left in the 36 hours or so since you've been away. So I went immediately to this location where I met him, and we stood on this hill and saw this sort of -- this sort of scene unfolding in front of us. It was actually Good Friday, I seem to remember that it was a bit of a funny old thing to have to be seeing on Good Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while you were at this border point with Mr. Ciaglinski, were you able to obtain any information as to why these persons that we see on the photograph that are in the field had crossed the border into Macedonia? Why they had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because among all of these people were some of our former security guards who made themselves known to us, and we had interpreters with us anyway, so we were able to ask various people that came up to -- people came up to the road because although they weren't aloud onto the road, there were a number of water bowsers, and their only way of getting drinking water was to get water from the water bowsers. So they would come up with empty soft drinks bottles, plastic bottles, and fill their water containers. And at that point we were able to ask them what their situation was. Many of them said that they were from Pristina, that they had been rounded up at very short notice and moved down to the station where they were loaded onto the train, that the train took them down to the border where they were ordered off the train and were ordered to walk down the train lines to this location, and further were told that the area either side of the train lines was mined and therefore if they strayed from the train tracks, they would doubtless be blown up. The other thing we were told was that as they were leaving at various moments during this process, they were systematically robbed and their identification documents were taken off them, and it was certainly the case that almost everybody that we met had no identification documents because it became obviously a serious issue later when we were attempting to help some of these people be taken to countries of refuge and they needed new identity documents to be created for them, and we were involved in that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say that the -- many of these persons told you they were from Pristina and they had been rounded up at very short notice. Did they tell you anything as to who had been involved in rounding them up and moving them to the train station?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was largely a police operation. They said that they were -- that the police entered their locality, banged on all the doors, told everybody that they had 5 minutes to get out, and then herded everybody down to the station. But it was largely described as a police operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken about these persons saying that they had been systematically robbed and that their identification documents had been taken from them. What was, in your view, the significance of that, of the removal of the identification documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was to render them stateless. Throughout -- throughout the Balkan wars, the issue of who someone is and where he comes from and how he can establish who he is and where he comes from has been raised many times, and this was the first time I had had direct experience of coming across this myself. But it was a consistent complaint of these people, that they had -- had had their ID taken from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the period of the end of the conflict in 1999. Did you return to Kosovo after the conflict ended?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When exactly did you return?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived the day before KFOR went into Kosovo, attached to the KFOR headquarters led by General Mike Jackson, and took Richard Ciaglinski with me. So he and I went in as an additional liaison team to assist the KFOR when it went in. We arrived, as I say, the day before the -- the force went in, and on the day that the force went in, I personally went in with General Jackson; and then the day after that, I took -- I led the whole of the UN convoy into Kosovo by road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say that you arrived the day before the KFOR went in and that you later also went in with General Jackson. To which locality specifically did you go when you returned to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On D day, on the day that the forces first went in, I went into Pristina airport and then flew back out -- back down to Macedonia. And the day, after I went with the UN convoy up to Pristina and we then stayed in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to staying in Pristina during this time. Can you just very briefly tell us about your observations in the town when you returned in this period to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day I arrived, my job was to go to the Grand Hotel and to attend a meeting with the Serb military that was taking place in the basement of the Grand Hotel. I did that, I suppose, about 7.00 at night. And having finished that meeting at about half past 8.00 at night, I walked around that area between -- between the Grand Hotel and where the OSCE building had been because that was where many of the government buildings had been. I really wanted to see what the state of the building that the OSCE had been in. And in walking around there, Richard Ciaglinski drew my attention to a bonfire which was burning. Do you want me to describe this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was outside the public part of the police headquarters on the opposite side of the road to the Grand Hotel. And a bonfire, a conical shaped heap of stuff was smouldering about two and a -- about a metre high. We warmed our hands at it because it was a chilly night, and then to get a bit more flame we kicked at it. And as the bonfire sort of fell apart, we realised it was actually a bonfire of identity documents. And so we retrieved some of the documents and realised that the whole bonfire was actually a bonfire of burning identity documents of various sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to ascertain to whom these identity documents belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got several of these, I suppose about half a dozen, and put the fire out. And it was clear that they were Kosovar Albanians. The dates of birth varied, but I think the earliest was about 1950, and the I think there was one as late at 1970. But generally they belonged to Kosovar Albanians of an age where they would still be alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you one last exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 00407. If we could have that up on the screen. This is a document that is called the Blue Book. OSCE Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while that is being brought up, just to follow up from your last answer, do you know who was burning the documents outside the MUP building? Were you able to find that out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean nobody was coming out to stack up the fire and throw a few more on it while we were there. I think we might have asked him what in the heck he was doing. We passed the documents and that information to the Royal Military Police Detachment of the headquarters of the KFOR since obviously at that stage there were no civilian police -- international civilian police on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I see we now have the document up on the screen. Do you -- are you familiar with this document, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, the Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Blue Book was a briefing document whose purpose was to attempt to show where things were happening. Each morning there was a daily update for the head of mission and the deputies given by -- in the presence of all of the heads of the staff branches. And this began as a -- a written description of what was going on. But since not all of the senior members of the mission were familiar with the area outside of Pristina, it became clear that we needed to present this information more visually, and also to give some value to the reports that were being offered. So we tried to show where there were clusters of activity, and we tried to show how authentic we felt -- how reliable we felt the information was. So it was -- it was not just a straight description of what had happened, but a description with a commentary which attempted to say that this is rather unusual, or this is following the trend, or this looks very similar to something that we saw a week ago but in another location. So the commentary on it was part of the value added that we attempted to give to it. And it was put together by the fusion cell, which was the cell which was not receiving all of the information on a minute-by-minute basis, but it was what stepped back one step and was trying to analyse all of this open source information that came to us from all of the regional centres, from all sources. And to try to collate it and make sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned having tried to show how authentic the information was and reliable you felt it was. How did you go about trying to check the reliability of the information before including it in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used a system which is -- has generally been used in military intelligence which is to rate it from A1 to F6 with the A to F rating being the reliability of the source and 1 to 6 being the likelihood of it being correct. And so an A1 report would be something from a source you knew very well and you trusted him and it was entirely probable that this was -- that this was correct because it had maybe been checked with another source and found to be correct. On the other hand, if someone sidles up to you in a cafe and whispers something and you've never seen him before in your life and it sounds most improbable, then the man with the board on the street who says the world is going to end tomorrow is probably F6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go through some of the entries of this book just so we can all understand what sort of information was included there and how it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could first turn to page 247 of the English, and in the B/C/S version this is page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is an entry that's entitled "Significant Events As Reported" and the date is 15th January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the witness could only have the English displayed for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we zoom it up, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I indicated the B/C/S version was page 24 just for reference for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So we see in this page we have six events that are indicated. Could you explain what this is that we see here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the visual depiction of what's been going on throughout Friday the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could pause a moment, please. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it possible for me to have this page so that I can follow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not only possible, you should let us try and ensure you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I think if you could continue, if I could again request for the witness only to display the English so he can be able to read what it on the page. Thank you. So, General, just if you could just continue with the answer you were giving about the explanation of what we see here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need the font up, I'm afraid. Otherwise you're going to see me half an inch away from the screen. Great. Okay. Number 1, Regional Centre 3, that's Pec, report the contact between the VJ and MUP and the KLA forces continued in the vicinity of Gornji Ratis and Donji Ratis which as you can see is due south of Pec. Number 2, two of my people are wounded by small-arms fire and glass fragments in approximately the same area, and we later discovered that the wounds were not life threatening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, sir. What I was -- what my question was aimed at was just for you to explain how this information would have been compiled by the fusion cell --

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- more than the actual -- because we can read what is on the page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly couldn't when it was down half a page size. Yeah. The reports came into the operations cell which was dealing with the reports as they came in. They logged them, they informed people that needed to be told; and if they needed to adjust who send people to look at things or reinforce a presence, then they gave those instructions. And they noted it in a written log, sort of one serial after another, so it was chronological. So if something happened at midday at the left-hand end of Kosovo and something happened at 12.01 at the right-hand end, they would appear in the log one after the other. It was all passed to the fusion centre who mapped it all on the map and then attempted to say what was going on in the broader picture. So the fact that Serial 1 and Serial 2 are in the same area, they could well have been -- the reports to those thing could well have been four hours apart, so they could have been four pages away on the log. So bringing it all together on the map and showing exactly where things are is an attempt to show where the hot spots are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now turn to page 251 of the English and this is 25 in the B/C/S. And I would again ask for the English to be displayed for the witness and if we could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry entitled "Significant Events as Reported," and it's --

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- number 5. We see that this is a report from RC 1 of an attack by combined VJ MUP forces in thee vicinity of Stimlje, and there are several localities mentioned there including the village of Racak. Yesterday you had spoken about an incident in the village of Racak; would this entry be a reference to that same incident that you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes. It was -- it came from RC 5, which wasn't Prizren. It was -- it was one that was further to the east and had only just been set up. But yes, and again, this is a precis of obviously a day's worth of events packaged together to try to put a consistent narrative together. So it's really everything we knew about what had gone on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have page 563 up on the screen, and this is page 42 on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry that is entitled "Significant Events As Reported," and it's dated 21 February, 1999. And on the top we see "RC 3 large VJ convoy spotted." I believe that's still not up on the screen. Do you have that up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. We see that in this entry there's a reference to a large convoy of -- a VJ convoy of Serbs travelling south from Belgrade heading towards Nis and presumably on towards Kosovo. And it says: "There is no indication that the convoy ever turned back to Belgrade." How were you able to obtain this sort of information, that a large convoy was travelling towards Kosovo, a VJ convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was because one of my vehicles was on the main -- was going to or from Belgrade. Obviously we went -- people went up to Belgrade for various reasons. We had a liaison office in Belgrade as well which was our foot on the ground in Belgrade; a point of contact in Belgrade. And so for a number of reasons, people drove from Kosovo up the highway to Belgrade which took about four hours. And this was a sighting that was -- that was obviously made by the -- I think by a vehicle going in the opposite direction. So I think that as it was going north towards Belgrade, it observed this convoy, checked what was on it, and reported it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this would have been an observation made by one of your verifiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have further information as to what happened to this convoy, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can now turn to page 703 in the English; and in the B/C/S this is page 74.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry dated "Significant Events as Reported," 12 March, 1999. And the heading of it is "RC 2 Houses Burning Near Vucitrn." Now, yesterday you spoke about a large-scale offensive in the Kacanik and Vucitrn areas, and you told us how you yourself went to Vucitrn to see what was happening. Does this entry relate to the same operation, or is this a different incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's an earlier part of the operation I then went and observed. The specific location here that's indicated is to the south and east of where I went; and when I went it was at least the next day. But I think it was part of the same operation which was -- which was over quite a large area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that at the end of the first paragraph we have an A1. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A1 means that it's been verified on the ground by people whom we trust, by more than one source.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This refers to the system that you have referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have page 735 up on the screen; and in the B/C/S this is page 85.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is an entry for the 14th March, 1999, and the heading says: "Heavy Fighting in Southern Part of Klina." I wanted to ask you, this entry indicates that there's heavy fighting in a number of localities and speaks about the type of fighting that has been observed. And there's a comment included in there, and I wanted to ask you about the source of this comment.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be a comment inserted by the fusion cell when they had got the report and they had compared it with all the other reports they had, and would wish to put it in context for the people that were being briefed. So it's a comment by the fusion cell sitting in Pristina on something that happened some way away that they didn't personally observe, but they had got other reports from other sources which were relevant and so they put the whole thing together with a comment. And when it says "comment," it's an opinion; but it's an opinion by somebody who is a professional at doing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that -- I see that in the comment it says, second sentence, The MUP said that they had not been involved - and the third sentence - However MUP, including PJP milicija were observed by RC 3 operating in the the area. Why was this significant and why has -- do you know why PJP has been highlighted there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, PJP is rather more competent. In other words, it's not your average MUP who would have been garrisoning, for instance, a fixed position like Malisevo. PJP milicija are the more competent units of better people, better trained, and able to be deployed throughout the area, not necessarily specifically tied to a particular location, but deployed to areas of greater need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have page 851 up on the screen; and this is 147 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry for 26 March, 1999, and it's -- the heading is "Djakovica Burning." Now, my question about this entry is that it's dated after the period that you and your verifiers left Kosovo. So I would like you to explain to the Court how you were able to continue reporting what was going on on the ground after you had left.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left mobile phones -- no, we didn't leave mobile phones. The people that worked for us all had mobile phones, all had their own mobile phones, and generally we knew what those mobile phones were. And so we were able to ring our former civilian employees, both Albanian and Serb, and say to them, What's going on? And we received quite a lot of reports that way. Six days after we left, we were still in contact with quite a lot of these people, and so this would be a report or a report compiled from a number of reports which -- which appeared to indicate what was going on on the ground. The fact that we've rated it C3 as opposed to A1 mean's that we were absolutely not convinced it was all exactly as described, and it was a useful way of reminding ourselves that this is not firsthand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the comment on this page says: "The pattern continues in outlying towns as well as in Pristina. Initially, it was thought that the major cities would be spared, however, that appears not to be the case now." What would have been the source of this information? Would that have again been information you obtained on the ground from persons who were there in the province?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the comment "it was thought the major cities would be spared" reflects the fact that in the first few days the action of the Serb forces was in the areas where the KLA appeared to be concentrated, i.e., not in the cities. And so to start with, we saw a pattern of activity by the Serb forces in the country-side, and then we see this change and they start to clear out the Albanians from the cities as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Just the last entry I want to show you in this document is page 855; and it's 149 in the B/C/S. And this is also an entry for the same date, 26 March, 1999; and it's an entry entitled "Armed Serb Civilians Patrolling Pristina." Now, we see that this entry says - I think it's up on the screen now - it is reported that there were groups of armed Serb civilians patrolling through the city of Pristina. And that there had been reports of looting and burning of Albanian houses and businesses throughout the city and also of these civilians participating murders of Albanian civilians. And we see that it has the same rating as the previous page. So would the source of this information again have been from your sources on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the comment that's included in this entry. It says: "The VJ and MUP had allowed lawlessness to get out of hand." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time I probably chastised the author and said that's a blinding glimpse of the obvious. But given that we are where we are today, I think it's very apposite that they wrote it. But clearly they are reporting on the fact that what is taking place is not an operation by people attempting to promote the rule of law by going after criminals and detaining criminals in the KLA, that the the local Serb population or elements of the local Serb population have been allowed to join in the overall lawlessness and persecution of the Albanian civilians in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for the witness. I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. This is 00407. I know that my learned colleague from the Defence had raised an objection, and I would like to clarify our position regarding this document. Since my learned colleague very rightly so yesterday raised the issue of the lack of translations in the e-court system for this exhibit, these have now been located and uploaded and the full set has been provided to the Defence. It is my understanding that only a few of them had been previously disclosed and the full set was provided yesterday and is now in the e-court system. We had made a selection of the pages we wanted to have admitted. These sum up approximately to 160 pages, so this is a very lengthy document. Of course, I can't go through each page with the witness and have him comment on them, but I would request that based on the evidence he has given on how this document was compiled and what sort of information is contained within the document, I would request that Your Honours receive that portion that has been translated into evidence. It is our view that this document contains contemporaneous reports of what was going on on the ground and that it will assist Your Honours in having an overview of events for the dates that are included within the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, are you saying that 160 pages have now been translated and are in the e-court system, or are you saying the whole of the book has been translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Only 160 pages have been translated. This was a selection that was made in the Milutinovic case when the same document was used, and these are the pages that we have also selected to rely on in this case. So the whole document has not been translated. The reason for that is that it's a very lengthy document and of course we know that CLSS has very limited resources and the document has almost 1.000 pages. So we did not request the entirety of the document to be translated, only -- and the number I'm giving of 160 pages is an approximate number, Your Honours. It's -- we have prepared a spreadsheet which indicates all the pages that we intend to rely upon and that have translations which are now in the e-court system. And we are happy to provide that to the Registry Officer and the Defence at a convenient time so the relevant pages can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many of these had been provided and translated for before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's my understanding that less than 10. I do have to check that, but that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you explain why not 160?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is something a bit difficult to explain, Your Honour. I was under the impression the entirety of the translations had been disclosed because, as I said, this is material we had in the Milutinovic case. However, when my learned colleague raised this issue yesterday, which in fact came as a surprise to me, because I wasn't aware that this was the situation, we did run a check in our system and did not find that these translations had been provided. The explanation that was given to me is, by one of our assistants, is that these translations have been re-stamped with a different reference number and so they didn't come up as directly linked to this document when a search was run in the system. So for some reason, I can't explain why this re-stamping was done, but this is the explanation I was able to obtain yesterday. And they have all-- they were all put together yesterday during the course of this witness's evidence and were provided at the end of yesterday's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you want to tender the whole book but you've uploaded into e-court the 160 pages you wish to rely upon. Have I got that clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, our view, Your Honour, is that it will assist the Chamber to have the whole book just in terms of context, but having regard to the objection raised by my learned colleague, we are -- we would agree to only tender the portions that have been translated because I am aware that my learned colleague has not had the opportunity to review in B/C/S the portions that have not been translated. So we would be willing to agree to tender only the translated portions which approximately sums up to 160 or so pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I still need to know more. Can you tell me the dates of the first and the last of the entries in the book?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The first entry, it starts in December 1998 and the last one is early April 1999, so it covers that entire period. I didn't start showing -- to show the witness from the first entry because simply I wanted to draw and get the witness comments on specific entries which are the ones we've seen today, but that is specifically the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the original reports are all in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, the entire document is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I even more object now after what we heard from the witness and from the Prosecution. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this an A1 objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. We are on a very slippery ground. I don't mean in a bad way. We are dealing here with intelligence professionals who are providing opinions and conclusions in this book. However, this is the only thing that can be done by the Chamber. I'm not talking about confidential material, but the value of everything else will be weighed and valued by the Chamber. But as I said, we are on a slippery ground and I intend to address this issue in more detail with the witness. If we adopt this approach, then we would have lots and lots of document of the same nature that do not only relate to the Kosovo Verification Mission but would also involve the activities of intelligence services of other countries; the conclusions of the EU Observation Mission, and their respective services. And I think that that would be the basic objection that I have. As for the rest, not a single page of this document according to 65 ter has been translated, if my memory serves me well, I'm not sure. None of the pages from the Blue Book has been admitted in the Milutinovic case, so this is where this error may have stemmed from, and this mistake was just today revealed and detected. How is it possible that the service, the CLSS failed to translate this document over the period of ten years? And what I'm even more fascinated by is that suddenly yesterday we received 200 pages during this witness's testimony for me to review and to prepare myself for cross-examination. I just randomly found and recognised a page that I've seen elsewhere, but having all this in mind, I am afraid that the Defence might not be fully prepared to deal with this witness and act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can very briefly be allowed to reply to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you've had a fair enough go, Ms. Kravetz. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will not receive either the Blue Book or the 160 pages as exhibits at the present time. It will mark both of them separately for identification. It will listen, of course, attentively to your cross-examination, Mr. Djurdjic. At the end of that, the position may be clearer; or it may be that it will be necessary to give this matter further consideration later in the course of the trial, in the light of your full consideration of the materials that are there, and possibly other evidence that touches upon it. So at the moment, they will be marked for identification. You will, of course, in your cross-examination deal with them as you think appropriate, Mr. Djurdjic. Is that clear enough for your purposes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore the book which is 65 ter 407 will become Exhibit P1028 marked for identification. And the excerpt of 160 pages will become Exhibit P1029 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you ready to commence now, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. I am assisted by Ms. Marie O'Leary, also a member of our team. May I kindly ask you, since you are a fast talker, as am I, to wait for the typing on the LiveNote to finish before you start answering so that the interpreters and court reporters can do their job properly. I would also appreciate it if you could give me precise and concise answers to save time. So far you have given a number of statements and I have read them all. You also testified twice. That's why I will try to ask only questions that have not been asked before and concentrate on points that are of special interest to us. But there's one thing that intrigues me: In your 2000 statement I have not found this point where you speak about the large number of people on the border of Macedonia, the bad situation they were in, et cetera. How come you as a human being did not find it important enough to mention in 2000 when you were giving the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was so recent that it was a constant back-drop to everything that was going on at the time. I certainly was deeply affected by it. I have got at home photos of me actually there, if you doubt whether I was there or not; but if I didn't mention it specifically in 2000, it was because the question did not come up. And I think at the end of the week in which I gave that statement in 2000 we felt we had probably suffered enough at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just opened up another issue. How did it come about that you gave a statement in 2000?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was approached by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia, and was asked to make a statement, so I made a statement. I checked with my superiors because I was still a serving officer, and they agreed it was the appropriate thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did the UK or the UK armed forces give you a waiver from the Official Secrets Act? Did you communicate absolutely everything to the investigators, and are you able to share with us all the information you have today without any restrictions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been given no restriction from the official secrets -- no, no waivers from the Official Secrets Act; and I have tried not to breach the Official Secrets Act. Luckily, almost everything we did in Kosovo relied on open-source information; and while at the time I grumbled that I was getting very little background or specific intelligence material, it's actually quite an advantage when it comes to moments like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not quite understand this, but let's move on. When you were giving that first statement in 2000, what kind of documentation did you use?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the course of a week, I sat with -- with the investigator who had been sent -- sent to England who had, I seem to remember, two assistants, and we sat for about six hours a day, and he -- he went through everything, and it was taken down pretty much verbatim. And it was then produced for me, and I went through it and agreed that that was a true record of what had been stated over the course of about five days. So we went through things, it was recorded, it was typed up, I went through it again, agreed that was an accurate description of what I had said, and we put the statement together that way. That's why it's so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it a spontaneous account on your part, or did you receive from the investigator a list of topics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigator wanted to specifically focus on certain issues, asked me to focus on certain issues which I did. But broadly I had -- I had most of the documents that I referred to myself and offered them to the investigators. The investigators were not able to offer me any documents to help me, as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents you were using, were they your own private documents or were they official documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a mixture. The notebooks that I used that I made my contemporaneous notes in were obviously my -- my notebooks. But from time to time I would glue into them, as you have seen, useful briefing notes that were made for me by my staff. The daily updates, the Blue Book, were all documents which were open documents within the headquarters; so while they were official documents, they were unclassified. They were not in any way confidential. They were made available to -- in the most part to Vienna, to the 54 participating countries of the OSCE, and so they were pretty widely available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this. Weren't the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission intended for Vienna?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that were sent up to Vienna, the daily reports were sent up for the Permanent Council, and for the Secretariat in Vienna. That's where they were prepared for, and that's where they went. And as part of that, they were distributed among the 54 delegations which were the participating states of the OSCE. So they were widely distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And outside that circle of users, others were or were not able to get hold of those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were. We routinely passed them to the NATO headquarters in Kumanovo in Macedonia because it was part of our responsibility to liaise with them as well since they were -- they were conducting the air Verification Mission, if you recall, so we passed our reports to them. We passed them to the EU Monitoring Mission. And frankly, if anybody else asked for them, we passed them to those people as well, if asked. I've certainly got no doubt that they probably even found their way to Belgrade despite the fact that at the time Serbia was not in the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then conclude that you did not forward your reports to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that the mission forwarded the reports to Belgrade. If the mission had been asked for the reports by Belgrade, then that would have been considered. It may actually have happened, but I'm not aware of it. And I'm certainly not aware of any request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to go back to the documents you used. Were these documents kept in your own private premises or in some office?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were kept in my garage in cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see here in paragraph 10 you mention Captain Rupert Witherow, Mr. John Harding, and the librarian of the British Army Historical Branch. Did you use any of their documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, when I returned from Kosovo to the UK in April of 1999, I was required to write a report which was a separate report for the UK government. And to do that, I had to do it inside Ministry of Defence premises. The premises used were the Army Historical Branch; and while I was doing that, my notebooks were indeed secured in locked containers inside the Army Historical Branch for the ten days that it took me to write that report. Rupert Witherow was one of my staff in Kosovo. John Harding was the appropriate official of the Army Historical Branch. The report I wrote is not part of the the documents that this Court has seen because it is classified, and it is subject to the Official Secrets Act.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these documents of yours, were they ever kept in Whitehall or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personal -- the nine personal books were in my possession the entire time, apart from the period that I was writing that report, which was about ten days. And during those ten days, as I have indicated, they were kept within a locked safe inside Whitehall. Apart from that, they've been with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when exactly were you writing that report, those ten days?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it was the last week of April, 1999, immediately after I had -- I had left the mission. I left the mission, I think, on the 24th of April. And I think it was the week immediately following that and ran into I think the first couple of days of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then those documents were returned to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I had access to them obviously when I was writing the report. It was simply a case of them being kept secure in the -- inside the Ministry of Defence overnight because I was not sleeping on the floor in the Ministry of Defence overnight during that period, I was going home every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That must be standard procedure. Why did you then mention Whitehall and these assistants of yours, your staff members, when you were giving the statement in 2000?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because as part of the -- as part of the preamble as we were sitting talking about the statement, this was one of the issues that was thought to be possibly significant by the investigator at the time. You will note that it's very early on in the statement, so this would have been something that we discussed in the first morning probably. How relevant it was to him, I don't know. It wasn't particularly relevant to me. And it's not a piece of the statement that I ever dwell upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during this interview with the investigators, you provided a large number of documents, at least that's what's stated in the statement itself, as we see in paragraphs 20 to -- in the last 20 to 22 paragraphs. From what source did these documents come from, the documents you were using or were shown during the interview?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were my personal archive. Each day I would receive a copy of these documents as part of my duties. They would come first to me because it was one of my staff branches that had initiated them, and so I would review them before they -- they were presented to the head of mission and to the morning meeting. And I would then -- I would then keep if not that copy, a copy, in one of the files. I think some of them were on disk and I then printed them out. But Rupert Witherow, the captain who you've referred to, was working directly for me at the time; and one of his duties was to make sure that we kept all of the documentation against such a moment as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excellent, you see that it was a good idea. But let me understand this correctly, it was your private documentation that you showed to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two sets of documents. One was the official document such as the daily reports, which I routinely had a copy of, which were the public documents. The private documents were the nine booklets that I retained which were my working booklets, which were my personal -- my personal notes. I certainly referred to those in my -- when I was making my statement in 2000; and where appropriate, they took photocopies of the relevant pages and they have been made available to the Court where appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood that part very well. But it means you were providing documents from your personal archive to the investigators, and the investigators took them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took copies of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, how did they make copies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stood at the photocopier and pressed print. That's how you make copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's about hard copies. What about computer copies, electronic copies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where some of the reports were on disks, I printed off copies of the appropriate -- I had printed off copies of the appropriate papers. They simply photocopied those papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we begin? General, I'm looking here at your brilliant professional career. What I'm interested in is to hear how it came about that you became an officer in the UK army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in the UK; I am a UK citizen. I applied to join the army as an officer. It required a waiver by the secretary of state because my father had not been born in England. That waiver was given and that enabled me to enter Sandhurst as an officer cadet in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in this last part particularly. Was that a secondary military school or was it a military academy, higher education institution that you joined?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a two-year course which had six terms, the first and last of which was military, and the middle four were one-third military and two-thirds academic in order to help us prepare to go to university.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that a civilian university or a military university?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the two years at Sandhurst, I was commissioned and after one year with soldiers went to Cambridge university, a civilian university, where I studied engineering because I was a member of the Royal Engineers. So the whole of my military education in effect took six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you finished your education, which rank were you given?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lieutenant. I was a 2nd lieutenant when I finished at Sandhurst in July 1966 after two years training at what was a military academy, if that's what you're asking. And then I spent one year with soldiers and I then went to Cambridge university as a serving officer. And during that period I took the exam to be promoted from 2nd lieutenant to lieutenant and was promoted lieutenant, I think, 18 months after being commissioned as 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not very familiar with military matters so therefore don't be surprised at the questions that I'm asking you. This academy that you finished, was that the army academy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was called the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst and was the place of military education for officers who were granted -- who were applying for a regular commission, that is, a career commission which would be the start of a career to the age of 55. There was another academy where a shorter course went on at the time called Mons and that was for officers who were going to do short-service commissions and who would have a shorter career in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what is your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two military specialties. One is as staff officer, and the original one was as a military engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you finished your studies at Cambridge, you were, I suppose, working as an officer. With what kind of units were you working?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a lieutenant and a captain I worked with engineer units. I then went to the army staff college for a year, where we learned to be staff officers and we learned more of all of the other pieces of the army. I then -- my career then alternated between positions doing staff work and positions commanding engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, did you serve all the time in Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I served in the Persian Gulf, in Canada, in Germany, in Norway, and eventually in Bosnia, and then in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your mission in Kosovo and the time spent there as well as in Bosnia, do you perceive that as part of your military career or as part of your civilian career?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a serving British officer until March 2001, and so when I was in Bosnia, I was a serving British officer working within a NATO headquarters and later working for the civilian high representative. And then in Kosovo I was a serving British officer seconded to our foreign office, our ministry of Foreign Affairs; and further seconded to the Vienna; and further seconded to the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission; but I remained a serving officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you in the Persian Gulf and why were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 1971. I was commanding a unit of 44 engineers in the Persian Gulf and down in Oman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you were only British forces there where you served or were there NATO force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were British, I was commanding a British unit; but in Oman there were also Omani forces that were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you mentioned being in Germany for a certain period of time. Can you give me the time frame and in which unit or formation did you serve?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From February 1967 until September 1967 I was a 2nd lieutenant in the 2nd division engineer battalion. From December 1978 until -- until December 1980, I was the chief operational logistics officer of the headquarters third armoured division in Soest, Germany. Then for two years immediately after that, I was an engineer company commander in the 26th engineer battalion in Soest, Germany. And then in -- from July 1995 until October 1996, I was a major general on the staff of the headquarters allied land forces central Europe which was a NATO headquarters situated in Heidelberg, Germany. At that point I deployed to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you promoted to the rank of major-general?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if the translation was good. Were you speaking about East Germany or West Germany when you discussed your time there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1967 and from 1978 until 1982 I was in West Germany. By the time I went back to Germany in 1995, Germany had been unified, so there was only one Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard in the translation on the East Germany, that's why I wanted to clarify this with you. General, throughout this whole period and throughout your military career were you ever in the employ of any security service?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the exception of the Kosovo Verification Mission and Colonel Ciaglinski, did you throughout any of the periods that you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel hasn't finished the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You appear to have stopped mid-sentence. Something isn't completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished, but probably I wasn't heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Throughout your military career, with the exception of the Kosovo Verification Mission had you ever worked with Colonel Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I had met him in early 1995 when he was the assistant defence attache in Warsaw, Poland. And I visited Poland and the Polish chief engineer as part of my duties as chief engineer of the British army. So that's when I had met him before. I was aware of his existence before because of his name which has similar roots to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that you were the head of the department for NATO support, that was in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived there in August 1995 in a headquarters which was a NATO headquarters and where there were two major-generals, one responsible for operations, and one for support. I was the major-general responsible for all support aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you returned to Heidelberg in 1997. Which post did you hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held -- I went back to the same post. While I was in Sarajevo, I was the Chief of Staff of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, from 23rd of April until 13th of June 1999, which posts did you hold during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the senior army teacher at Royal College of Defence Studies in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after the 27th of June, 1999, until retirement, what jobs did you perform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to that post as the senior army member of the staff at the Royal College of Defence Studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you explain to us how it happened that in October 1998 you were dispatched to Vienna?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that a request was made by someone in the OSCE for a senior British officer with -- who was known to the OSCE to go and assist them, start their planning for the mission. Two names were asked for. The first one, his wife didn't let him go; and I was the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your wife let you go. Can you please tell me this: The British government actually sent you to Vienna, you didn't apply for this post like some other persons might have done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indicated that I was happy to go if asked for. There wasn't a post. On the day -- let me explain. On the day that the newspaper reports said that there was possibly going to be a mission put together by the OSCE, I spoke to my Ministry of Defence and said that if asked, I was prepared to go. This was not unusual since a similar process had happened a year earlier when I had been asked to go back to Bosnia to be the military advisor to the high rep. The reason I did this was that normally it is assumed that people will not be redeployed quickly after being deployed on an operation unless they are willing to be so deployed. So I needed to be a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, you were attached to the UK delegation in the OSCE, but were you sent there by the ministry or by the army? The Ministry of Foreign Affairs or by the army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but in order to be able to deploy me, they had to ask the Ministry of Defence. And so my minister of defence had to formally -- was formally requested by my minister of foreign affairs it he could borrow me, and he agreed to that. And I was called to the Ministry of Defence and literally walked with the minister of defence over to the minister of foreign affairs and, so to speak, handed over to the minister of foreign affairs personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well done. So two ministers dealt with you. Now, tell me, how did you become an OSCE official?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, as you describe, attached to the UK delegation in Vienna, and I was working to write a plan to put together the Kosovo Verification Mission to get it on the ground and operating as quickly as possible, because its mandate which was 12 months was already running. At some stage, Ambassador William Walker was nominated as the head of the mission and at some stage he asked to see me and asked if I would be prepared to join the OSCE Mission in Kosovo as one of his deputies. The matter was then referred to my Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I understand that the decision was made by the OSCE Permanent Council that I should be appointed a deputy head of the mission on the 2nd of November, although I was not actually told until a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that appointment went through, did you have any kind of former or legal relationship with the OSCE in terms of having a contract signed with them stipulating what your duties were going to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed a normal OSCE contract, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what were the terms and continues contained therein? What were your duties and obligations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- I mean, it was a normal contract that any person who is seconded by his nation to the OSCE signs which says that he will do what he is told by the head of mission, that he will not do anything that brings the OSCE into disrepute, and he will probably not make off with any OSCE property. I think those were the three things. I would need to be reminded of it, but it was a perfectly normal contract for any secondee from any nation being seconded to the OSCE, as opposed to a contract position where you worked directly for the OSCE without the intervention of your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand then that thereby you became an OSCE official, but you had to earn some money for a living while you were working for the OSCE. Who was paying your salary at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, during the period between October and your appointment, did you undergo any preparations in the interim period preceding your departure and arrival in Kosovo, and what kind of preparations if any you had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no preparation because I was -- I was rung up at 10.30 in the morning and asked if I was genuinely prepared to go to the OSCE when I was in England, and I said yes. And two hours later at 12.30 I was told to please get myself from where I was to the Ministry of Defence by 4.00 in afternoon so that I could be interviewed by the minister of defence. And as I've described, he marched me over to the minister of foreign affairs, handed me over there. And I was put in a vehicle with three other members of UK staff and we were taken to Royal Air Force Northolt, and we went to Vienna that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, could you just be briefer in your answers. You say you did not have any preparation in Britain, but did you have any preparation when you arrived in the OSCE in Vienna? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if I understood you correctly even at the beginning after you arrived in Vienna and the first time you were in Belgrade, almost no agreement was signed. Perhaps one was signed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original OSCE agreement between Geremek and the Yugoslav minister of foreign affairs whose name escapes me had been signed, and it was on that basis that we went down to Kosovo to see what -- what the situation looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was signed on the 16th, but it was known a while before that the agreement had been reached. You say that on the 17th October, 1998, you attended a meeting in Belgrade with Mr. John Sandrock; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us who John Sandrock is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he was in charge of administration and procurement as a contracted OSCE official.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was his occupation and what was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was American and he was in charge of the IT and logistics of all deployed OSCE missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Apart from you two, were there any other members of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the other members were and something about their profile?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I was trying to be brief. The other members, the key members, were a couple of the staff of John Sandrock because the purpose of this trip was to find out what the requirements were for support to enable the mission to operate inside Kosovo. Added to that, at the request of the contact group were, I think, two members from each contact group -- two people from each contact group mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please give me brief answers, I'll ask more sub-questions, that's better than having a long answer. Am I right in thinking that the Yugoslav side was interested in the contents and the method of verification that you were planning on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
